title: Value Type
content:
What Does It Mean to Be a Value Type in C++?#What does it really calling something a value type in C++?
A value type behave like int or double. Lets take int as a reference point. With int, a wide range of of operations work by default:
x = y //assignment int z = x; // copy constructor x==y // comparison do_nothing(x) // pass by value (copy ctor) if(x){} // truth test - implicit conversion to bool x+y // arithmetic x +=y // compound assignment x++ // mutation (postfix operator) These operations define what value type means in practice. This is the baseline
A User-Defined Type#struct complex { int real; int imaginary; };some operations still work:
complex x = y; // copy assignment x = y // assignment do_nothing(x) //copy ctor these work because the compiler generates the special member functions automatically. Copy construction and copy assignment are provided member wise. but this is where the similarity to int ends
where value semantics are missing?#the following operations will fail:
x == y // equality operator if(x) // -> check this later which operator is it actully uses x+ y // no arithmetic x+=y // no compound operations The compoiler does invent meaning for these operations.
What a value types is#It is a type whose operations define its meaning:
what does equality mean what does addition mean is the type meaningful in boolean context? can it be modified destructively? (eg: x+=y) Built in types comes with these answers pre-defined
User-defined types do not.
Summary#what we must do to create value type:#When possible, value types should rely on compiler-generated special member functions (Rule of Zero), but value semantics do not depend on it (if the type own a resource: you must decide and define what copy means ans werite copy and assignment yourself) Explicitly define equality (operator==) if comparison makes sense Define arithmetic operators if the type participates in expressions Define compound operators for destructive updates Avoid hidden ownership or shared state A user-defined type can be copied and assigned by default because the compiler generates special member functions, but all higher-level value semantics must be explicitly defined.
